+`lem:pauli-observable-expansion`, paper `04_preliminaries.tex:1112-1159`. -/
+theorem primeTauObservable_mulVec_primePauliVec {p : ℕ} {K ι : Type*}
+    [Field K] [Fintype K] [DecidableEq K] [Fact p.Prime]
+    [Algebra (ZMod p) K] [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
+    (W : Bool) (a e : ι → K) :
+    primeTauObservable (p := p) W a *ᵥ primePauliVec (p := p) W e =
+      ffChar (p := p) (F := K) (dotProduct a e) •
+        primePauliVec (p := p) W e := by
+  classical
+  ext x
+  cases W with
+  | false =>
+      simp only [Matrix.mulVec_apply_eq_sum, primeTauObservable_Z_apply]
+      rw [Finset.sum_eq_single x]
+      · by_cases hxe : x = e
+        · subst e
+          simp [primePauliVec]
+        · simp [primePauliVec, hxe]
+      · intro y _ hy
+        simp [Ne.symm hy]
+      · simp
+  | true =>
+      simp only [Matrix.mulVec_apply_eq_sum, primeTauObservable_X_apply]
+      let y : ι → K := x - a
+      rw [Finset.sum_eq_single y]
+      · have hshift : x = y + a := by
+          funext i
+          simp [y]
+        rw [if_pos hshift, one_mul]
+        simp only [primePauliVec, if_true, Pi.smul_apply,
+          smul_eq_mul]
+        calc
+          (Real.sqrt (Fintype.card (ι → K) : ℝ) : ℂ)⁻¹ *
+                ffChar (p := p) (F := K) (-dotProduct e y) =
+              (Real.sqrt (Fintype.card (ι → K) : ℝ) : ℂ)⁻¹ *
+                ffChar (p := p) (F := K)
+                  (dotProduct a e + -dotProduct e x) := by
+            congr 2
+            simp only [y, dotProduct, Pi.sub_apply, mul_sub,
+              Finset.sum_sub_distrib]
+            rw [show (∑ i, a i * e i) = ∑ i, e i * a i by
+              apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
+              intro i _
+              exact mul_comm _ _]
+            abel
+          _ = (Real.sqrt (Fintype.card (ι → K) : ℝ) : ℂ)⁻¹ *
+                (ffChar (p := p) (F := K) (dotProduct a e) *
+                  ffChar (p := p) (F := K) (-dotProduct e x)) := by
+            rw [AddChar.map_add_eq_mul]
+          _ = _ := by ring
+      · intro z _ hz
+        rw [if_neg]
+        · simp
+        · intro hshift
+          apply hz
+          funext i
+          have hi := congrFun hshift i
+          simp only [Pi.add_apply] at hi
+          change z i = x i - a i
+          calc
+            z i = (z i + a i) - a i := by simp
+            _ = x i - a i := by rw [← hi]
+      · simp

+/-- Fourier expansion of a generalized Pauli observable in its common

+`04_preliminaries.tex:1112-1161`. -/
+theorem primeTauObservable_eq_sum_primePauliProj {p : ℕ} {K ι : Type*}
+    [Field K] [Fintype K] [DecidableEq K] [Fact p.Prime]
+    [Algebra (ZMod p) K] [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι] [Nonempty ι]
+    (W : Bool) (a : ι → K) :
+    primeTauObservable (p := p) W a =
+      ∑ e : ι → K,
+        ffChar (p := p) (F := K) (dotProduct a e) •
+          primePauliProj (p := p) W e := by
+  classical
+  ext x y
+  rw [show
+    (∑ e : ι → K,
+      ffChar (p := p) (F := K) (dotProduct a e) •
+        primePauliProj (p := p) W e) x y =
+      ∑ e : ι → K,
+        ffChar (p := p) (F := K) (dotProduct a e) *
+          primePauliProj (p := p) W e x y by
+        rw [Matrix.sum_apply]
+        rfl]
+  cases W with
+  | false =>
+      rw [primeTauObservable_Z_apply]
+      by_cases hxy : x = y
+      · subst y
+        simp [primePauliProj, primePauliVec, Matrix.vecMulVec_apply]
+      · simp [primePauliProj, primePauliVec, Matrix.vecMulVec_apply, hxy]
+  | true =>
+      rw [primeTauObservable_X_apply]
+      simp_rw [primePauliProj_X_apply]
+      have hsum :
+          (∑ e : ι → K,
+            ffChar (p := p) (F := K) (dotProduct a e) *
+              ((Fintype.card (ι → K) : ℂ)⁻¹ *
+                ffChar (p := p) (F := K) (dotProduct e (y - x)))) =
+            (Fintype.card (ι → K) : ℂ)⁻¹ *
+              ∑ e : ι → K,
+                ffChar (p := p) (F := K) (dotProduct e (a + y - x)) := by
+        rw [Finset.mul_sum]
+        apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
+        intro e _
+        calc
+          ffChar (p := p) (F := K) (dotProduct a e) *
+                ((Fintype.card (ι → K) : ℂ)⁻¹ *
+                  ffChar (p := p) (F := K) (dotProduct e (y - x))) =
+              (Fintype.card (ι → K) : ℂ)⁻¹ *
+                (ffChar (p := p) (F := K) (dotProduct e a) *
+                  ffChar (p := p) (F := K) (dotProduct e (y - x))) := by
+            rw [dotProduct_comm a e]
+            ring
+          _ = _ := by
+            rw [← AddChar.map_add_eq_mul]
+            congr 2
+            simp only [dotProduct, Pi.add_apply, Pi.sub_apply, mul_add, mul_sub,
+              Finset.sum_add_distrib, Finset.sum_sub_distrib]
+            abel
+      rw [hsum, sum_ffChar_dotProduct]
+      have hsupport : a + y - x = 0 ↔ x = y + a := by
+        constructor
+        · intro h
+          funext i
+          have hi : a i + y i - x i = 0 := by
+            simpa only [Pi.add_apply, Pi.sub_apply, Pi.zero_apply] using congrFun h i
+          calc
+            x i = a i + y i := (sub_eq_zero.mp hi).symm
+            _ = y i + a i := add_comm _ _
+        · intro h
+          funext i
+          have hi := congrFun h i
+          simp only [Pi.add_apply] at hi
+          change a i + y i - x i = 0
+          apply sub_eq_zero.mpr
+          rw [hi, add_comm]
+      by_cases hxy : x = y + a
+      · rw [if_pos hxy, if_pos (hsupport.mpr hxy)]
+        exact (inv_mul_cancel₀
+          (show (Fintype.card (ι → K) : ℂ) ≠ 0 by positivity)).symm
+      · rw [if_neg hxy, if_neg (fun h => hxy (hsupport.mp h))]

+    [Fintype K] [DecidableEq K] [Fact p.Prime] [Algebra (ZMod p) K]
+    [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι] [Nonempty ι] (W : Bool) :
+    (∑ e : ι → K, primePauliProj (p := p) W e) = 1 := by
+  have h := primeTauObservable_eq_sum_primePauliProj
+    (p := p) (K := K) (ι := ι) W (0 : ι → K)

+  rw [h]

+  intro e _
+  simp [dotProduct]

+theorem posSemidef_primePauliProj {p : ℕ} {K ι : Type*} [Field K]
+    [Fintype K] [DecidableEq K] [Fact p.Prime] [Algebra (ZMod p) K]
+    [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι] (W : Bool) (e : ι → K) :
+    (primePauliProj (p := p) W e).PosSemidef := by

+`eq:pauli-inversion-0` of blueprint `lem:pauli-observable-expansion`, paper

+    [Field K] [Fintype K] [DecidableEq K] [Fact p.Prime]
+    [Algebra (ZMod p) K] [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι] [Nonempty ι]
+    (W : Bool) (e : ι → K) :
+    primePauliProj (p := p) W e =
+      (Fintype.card (ι → K) : ℂ)⁻¹ •
+        ∑ a : ι → K,
+          ffChar (p := p) (F := K) (-dotProduct a e) •

+    rw [show
+      (∑ a : ι → K,
+        ffChar (p := p) (F := K) (-dotProduct a e) *
+          ffChar (p := p) (F := K) (dotProduct a b)) =
+        ∑ a : ι → K,
+          ffChar (p := p) (F := K) (dotProduct a (b - e)) by
+          apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
+          intro a _
+          rw [← AddChar.map_add_eq_mul]
+          congr 2

+  simp_rw [Finset.smul_sum, smul_smul]
+  rw [Finset.sum_comm]
+  simp_rw [← Finset.sum_smul]
+  simp_rw [hcoeff]
+  simp

/-!
# Generalized Pauli operators and EPR states

The definitions here use finite matrix entries and rank-one projectors, so they
are usable by the later game statements without introducing an abstract
operator algebra.  The observable/projector expansions are obtained from
finite-field Fourier orthogonality in characteristic two.

## References

The source-facing nodes are blueprint `def:lin-reg`, `def:EPR`,
`def:generalized-pauli`, and `lem:pauli-observable-expansion`.  The paper origin is
`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:908-1161`.

open MIPStarRE.Quantum
open MIPStarRE.LDT.Preliminaries

variable {K : Type*} [Field K] [Fintype K] [DecidableEq K]
  [Algebra (ZMod 2) K]

/-- The two generalized Pauli bases used by the test in blueprint
`def:generalized-pauli`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1052-1096`.
-/
inductive PauliKind where
  | X
  | Z
  deriving DecidableEq, Repr, Inhabited, Fintype

/-- The binary character used for generalized Pauli phases; see
`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1052-1081`.

It is public because the Fourier expansion declarations below expose this
character in their statement types. -/
noncomputable def phaseSign (t : ZMod 2) : ℂ :=
  if t = 0 then 1 else -1

/-- Formalization-only expansion of a sum over the binary field into its two
terms. -/
theorem sum_zmod_two {M : Type*} [AddCommMonoid M] (f : ZMod 2 → M) :
    ∑ b, f b = f 0 + f 1 := by
  calc
    ∑ b, f b = ∑ i : Fin 2, f (ZMod.finEquiv 2 i) := by
      exact Fintype.sum_equiv (ZMod.finEquiv 2).symm f
        (fun i : Fin 2 => f (ZMod.finEquiv 2 i)) (fun _ => rfl)
    _ = f (ZMod.finEquiv 2 0) + f (ZMod.finEquiv 2 1) := Fin.sum_univ_two _
    _ = f 0 + f 1 := by rfl

/-- Formalization-only case split for the binary field: every element is zero
or one. -/
theorem zmod_two_eq_zero_or_one (b : ZMod 2) : b = 0 ∨ b = 1 := by
  by_cases hb : b = 0
  · exact Or.inl hb
  · right
    have hval_ne : b.val ≠ 0 := (ZMod.val_ne_zero b).mpr hb
    have hval_lt : b.val < 2 := ZMod.val_lt b
    have hval : b.val = 1 := by omega
    exact (ZMod.val_eq_one (by omega) b).mp hval

/-- In characteristic two, the standard additive character is the sign
character used by the binary Pauli definitions. -/
theorem phaseSign_eq_ffChar (t : ZMod 2) :
    phaseSign t = ZMod.stdAddChar (N := 2) t := by
  by_cases ht : t = 0
  · subst t
    rw [phaseSign, if_pos rfl]
    exact (ZMod.stdAddChar (N := 2)).map_zero_eq_one.symm
  · have hval : t.val = 1 := by
      have hval_ne : t.val ≠ 0 := (ZMod.val_ne_zero t).mpr ht
      have hval_lt : t.val < 2 := ZMod.val_lt t
      omega
    have ht_one : t = 1 := (ZMod.val_eq_one (by omega) t).mp hval
    subst t
    rw [phaseSign, if_neg one_ne_zero]
    change (-1 : ℂ) = ZMod.stdAddChar (N := 2) ((1 : ℤ) : ZMod 2)
    rw [ZMod.stdAddChar_coe]
    convert Complex.exp_pi_mul_I.symm using 1
    all_goals ring_nf

/-- The binary sign character carries a sum to the product of the two signs.
This is the character property underlying blueprint
`def:generalized-pauli`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1052-1096`. -/
theorem phaseSign_add (s t : ZMod 2) :
    phaseSign (s + t) = phaseSign s * phaseSign t := by
  rw [phaseSign_eq_ffChar, phaseSign_eq_ffChar, phaseSign_eq_ffChar]
  exact (ZMod.stdAddChar (N := 2)).map_add_eq_mul s t

/-- The binary sign character takes real values, so conjugation fixes it. It is
used by the observable expansions of blueprint
`def:generalized-pauli`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1052-1096`. -/
theorem star_phaseSign (t : ZMod 2) : star (phaseSign t) = phaseSign t := by
  by_cases ht : t = 0 <;> simp [phaseSign, ht]

/-- The binary sign character squares to one, since the binary field has
characteristic two. This is the eigenvalue property used by the observables of
blueprint `def:generalized-pauli`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1052-1096`. -/
theorem phaseSign_mul_self (t : ZMod 2) : phaseSign t * phaseSign t = 1 := by
  rw [← phaseSign_add]
  have hzero : t + t = 0 := by
    rcases zmod_two_eq_zero_or_one t with ht | ht <;> subst ht <;> decide
  rw [hzero, phaseSign, if_pos rfl]

/-- The binary sign character sends sums to products. -/
theorem phaseSign_sum {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] (f : ι → ZMod 2) :
    phaseSign (∑ i, f i) = ∏ i, phaseSign (f i) := by
  classical
  induction (Finset.univ : Finset ι) using Finset.induction_on with
  | empty => simp [phaseSign]
  | @insert i s hi ih =>
      rw [Finset.sum_insert hi, Finset.prod_insert hi, phaseSign_add, ih]

omit [Fintype K] [DecidableEq K] in
/-- The product of the coordinate phases is the phase of the trace pairing. -/
theorem prod_phaseSign_binTrace_dotProduct {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι]
    (u v : ι → K) :
    ∏ i, phaseSign (binTrace K (u i * v i)) =
      phaseSign (binTrace K (dotProduct u v)) := by
  rw [← phaseSign_sum]
  congr 2
  simp [dotProduct]

/-- The complex amplitude `(√n)⁻¹` normalizing a uniform superposition over `n`
basis vectors squares to `n⁻¹`.

This formalization-only normalization identity supports the Pauli normalizer
of blueprint `def:EPR`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:908-950`, and the seed-fiber and
correlated-ancilla amplitudes of the direct low-degree transport. -/
theorem inv_sqrt_natCast_mul_self (n : ℕ) :
    (Real.sqrt (n : ℝ) : ℂ)⁻¹ * (Real.sqrt (n : ℝ) : ℂ)⁻¹ =
      (n : ℂ)⁻¹ := by
  calc
    (Real.sqrt (n : ℝ) : ℂ)⁻¹ * (Real.sqrt (n : ℝ) : ℂ)⁻¹ =
        ((Real.sqrt (n : ℝ) : ℂ) ^ 2)⁻¹ := by
      rw [pow_two, mul_inv_rev]
    _ = ((n : ℝ) : ℂ)⁻¹ := by
      rw [← Complex.ofReal_pow, Real.sq_sqrt (Nat.cast_nonneg n)]
    _ = (n : ℂ)⁻¹ := by norm_num

/-- Conjugated form of `inv_sqrt_natCast_mul_self`: the normalizing amplitude
`(√n)⁻¹` is real, so pairing it with its conjugate again gives `n⁻¹`.  This
formalization-only auxiliary is the form in which the identity occurs in Born
amplitudes, where the bra side carries the conjugate. -/
theorem inv_sqrt_natCast_mul_conj (n : ℕ) :
    (Real.sqrt (n : ℝ) : ℂ)⁻¹ *
        (starRingEnd ℂ) (Real.sqrt (n : ℝ) : ℂ)⁻¹ =
      (n : ℂ)⁻¹ := by
  rw [show (starRingEnd ℂ) (Real.sqrt (n : ℝ) : ℂ)⁻¹ =
      (Real.sqrt (n : ℝ) : ℂ)⁻¹ by simp]
  exact inv_sqrt_natCast_mul_self n

omit [Field K] [DecidableEq K] [Algebra (ZMod 2) K] in
private theorem pauliNormalizer_mul_self {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι]
    [DecidableEq ι] :
    (∏ _i : ι, (Real.sqrt (Fintype.card K : ℝ) : ℂ)⁻¹) *
        (∏ _i : ι, (Real.sqrt (Fintype.card K : ℝ) : ℂ)⁻¹) =
      (Fintype.card (ι → K) : ℂ)⁻¹ := by
  simp only [Finset.prod_const, Finset.card_univ]

    34	\section{Key theorem forms}
    35	Let $K$ be a finite extension of $\mathbb F_p$, let
    36	$\chi(x)=\exp(2\pi i\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb F_p}(x)/p)$, and let
    37	$a,a',b\in K^n$.  The relevant identities are
    38	\[
    39	 \tau^W(a)\tau^W(a')=\tau^W(a+a'),\qquad
    40	 \tau^W(a)^p=I,
    41	\]
    42	and
    43	\[
    44	 \tau^X(a)\tau^Z(b)=\chi(-a\mathbin{\cdot}b)
    45	 \tau^Z(b)\tau^X(a).
    46	\]
    47	The explicit shift and phase matrices are unitary. The second identity implies
    48	that every eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $\tau^W(a)$ satisfies $\lambda^p=1$. If
    49	$V\leq K^n$ and $v\notin V^\perp$, Fourier cancellation takes the form
    50	\[

    61	\section{Source and formal scope}
    62	The source defines the shift and phase matrices and states their product,
    63	$p$-th-power, unitarity, spectral, and twisted-commutation properties in
    64	\cite[lines 1056--1095]{Ji2020MIPStar}. It uses the same character for Fourier
    65	cancellation over a subspace at lines 1124--1132.  The single-qudit forward and
    66	inverse expansions occur at lines 1118--1139, and their multi-qudit forms occur
    67	at lines 1151--1161.  These assertions use the characteristic-$p$ character;
    68	they are not intrinsically binary.
    69	
    70	The formal definitions \path{primeTauShift}, \path{primeTauPhase}, and
    71	\path{primeTauObservable} use the canonical character \path{ffChar} in
    72	characteristic $p$.  Their theorem statements cover the product, power,
    73	unitarity, spectral, commutation, and cancellation identities for arbitrary
    74	$p$.  The declarations \path{primePauliVec}, \path{primePauliFourier}, and
    75	\path{primePauliProj} give the common eigenvectors, the Fourier matrix, and the
    76	rank-one projectors of the same source definition.  In particular, the $X$
    77	vector uses the negative phase $\chi(-e\cdot x)$, while
    78	\path{primeTauObservable_mulVec_primePauliVec} proves the positive-phase
    79	eigenvalue $\chi(a\cdot e)$.  Orthonormality, projectivity, positivity, and
    80	completeness are proved by the accompanying declarations in
    81	\path{MIPStarRE/QPBT/Algebra/PrimePauliBasis.lean}.
    82	
    83	The source assumptions are that $p$ is prime, $K=\F_q$ is a finite extension
    84	of $\F_p$, and the many-qudit carrier has positive finite dimension.  Lean
    85	encodes these by \path{Fact p.Prime}, a finite field $K$ with an algebra from
    86	\path{ZMod p}, and a finite decidable coordinate type $\iota$; the two
    87	source-labelled Fourier identities additionally assume \path{Nonempty}, which
    88	is exactly the condition $n\geq 1$.  The Boolean basis parameter uses
    89	\path{true} for $X$ and \path{false} for $Z$.  These are boundary encodings of
    90	the source domain, not additional mathematical hypotheses.
    91	
    92	The declarations whose names begin with \path{tauObservable} or use
    93	\path{phaseSign} remain the separately named specialization to $p=2$, where
    94	$\chi(x)=(-1)^{\operatorname{Tr}(x)}$.  This specialization is appropriate for
    95	the subsequent test, whose admissible sizes satisfy $q=2^k$; it is not
    96	substituted for the general statements.
    97	
    98	In characteristic two, $-x=x$, so the negative phase in the inverse expansion
    99	is the same \path{phaseSign} used in the forward expansion.  Thus
   100	\leanid{tauObservable\_eq\_sum\_pauliProj} and
   101	\leanid{pauliProj\_eq\_avg\_tauObservable} prove precisely the two displayed
   102	formulas for finite fields carrying an algebra over $\mathbb F_2$.  Their proof
   103	uses additive-character orthogonality after transporting the coordinate type
   104	along an equivalence with a finite ordinal; the restriction enters only through
   105	the identification of the canonical character with \path{phaseSign}.
   106	
   107	The proofs can be obtained directly from the displayed matrices.  A shift is a
   108	permutation matrix, a phase matrix has diagonal entries of modulus one, and a
   109	tensor product of such matrices is unitary.  Iterating the product identity
   110	gives $\tau^W(a)^p=I$.  Applying this equality to a nonzero eigenvector gives
   111	$(\lambda^p-1)v=0$, hence $\lambda^p=1$.  Finally, when
   112	$v\notin V^\perp$, the map $u\mapsto\chi(u\cdot v)$ is a nontrivial character
   113	of the finite additive group $V$, so its average vanishes.

1	\chapter{Algebraic preliminaries for the Pauli basis test}
     2	\label{chap:qpbt-algebra}
     3	
     4	This chapter records the algebraic preliminaries needed for the quantum Pauli
     5	basis test, following the preliminaries of \cite{Ji2020MIPStar}: subspace
     6	machinery over finite fields (which underlies the conditionally linear question
     7	distributions of Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-games}), field extensions, traces, and
     8	self-dual bases, the low-degree code, lines in $\F_q^m$, and the generalized
     9	Pauli observables together with the EPR states they act on. Measurements,
    10	strategies, and consistency relations for nonlocal games are treated in
    11	Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-games}; the test itself is defined in
    12	Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-test}.
    13	
    14	\section{Linear spaces and subspaces}
    15	% Paper label sec:linear-spaces kept for cross-reference fidelity.
    16	\label{sec:linear-spaces}
    17	
    18	Linear spaces are always of the form $V = \F^n$ for a finite field $\F$ and an
    19	integer $n \ge 1$, unless explicitly stated otherwise. We write $\hat{E} =
    20	\{\hat{e}_1, \dots, \hat{e}_n\}$ for the standard basis of $V$, where
    21	$\hat{e}_i$ has a $1$ in the $i$-th coordinate and $0$'s elsewhere, and
    22	$\mathrm{End}(V)$ for the set of linear maps from $V$ to itself.
    23	
    24	\begin{definition}[Register subspace]\label{def:register-subspace}
    25		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.registerSubmodule}
    26		\leanok
    27		A \emph{register subspace} $S$ of $V$ is a subspace that is the span of a
    28		subset of the standard basis of $V$. Such a subspace is represented by an
    29		indicator vector $u \in \{0,1\}^s$, where $s = \dim(V)$, via
    30		$S = \mathrm{span}\{\hat{e}_i : u_i = 1\}$.
    31	\end{definition}
    32	
    33	% The dot product itself is Mathlib's `dotProduct`; the Lean declaration listed here
    34	% is the orthogonal-subspace half of the node, which is the part this development
    35	% defines for itself.
    36	\begin{definition}[Dot product and orthogonal subspace]\label{def:dot-product-orthogonal}
    37		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.dotOrthogonal}
    38		\leanok
    39		For two vectors $u = \sum_{i=1}^n u_i \hat{e}_i$ and
    40		$v = \sum_{i=1}^n v_i \hat{e}_i$ in $V = \F^n$, the \emph{dot product} is
    41		\[
    42			u \cdot v = \sum_{i=1}^n u_i v_i \in \F\;.
    43		\]
    44		For a subspace $S$ of $V$, the \emph{subspace orthogonal to $S$ in $V$} is
    45		\[
    46			S^\perp = \bigl\{ u \in V : u \cdot v = 0 \text{ for all } v \in S \bigr\}\;.
    47		\]
    48		The notation $S^\perp$ leaves the ambient space $V$ implicit.
    49	\end{definition}
    50	
    51	Over finite fields, orthogonality lacks some of the familiar properties it has
    52	over $\R$ or $\C$; for example, a nonzero subspace may be orthogonal to itself,
    53	as is $\mathrm{span}\{(1,1)\}$ over $\F_2$. The following dimension identity
    54	nevertheless holds over every field.
    55	
    56	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:perp_perp}
    57		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.finrank_add_finrank_dotOrthogonal, MIPStarRE.QPBT.dotOrthogonal_dotOrthogonal}
    58		\leanok
    59		\uses{def:dot-product-orthogonal}
    60		Let $S$ be a subspace of $V$. Then $\dim(S) + \dim(S^\perp) = \dim(V)$, and
    61		\[
    62			(S^\perp)^\perp = S\;.
    63		\]
    64	\end{lemma}
    65	\begin{proof}
    66		\leanok
    67		\uses{def:dot-product-orthogonal}
    68		The elements of $S^\perp$ are the solutions of a feasible linear system whose
    69		coefficient matrix has $\dim(S)$ linearly independent rows, so the solution
    70		space has dimension exactly $\dim(V) - \dim(S)$. Every $u \in S$ is
    71		orthogonal to every element of $S^\perp$, so $S \subseteq (S^\perp)^\perp$.
    72		Applying the dimension identity twice shows that
    73		$\dim\bigl((S^\perp)^\perp\bigr) = \dim(S)$, so the inclusion is an equality.
    74	\end{proof}
    75	
    76	\begin{definition}[Complementary subspaces]\label{def:complementary}
    77		Two subspaces $S$ and $T$ of a linear space $V$ form a pair of
    78		\emph{complementary subspaces} of $V$ if
    79		\[
    80			S \cap T = \{0\}\;, \qquad S + T = V\;.
    81		\]
    82		In this case we write $V = S \oplus T$. Every $x \in V$ can be written
    83		uniquely as $x = x^S + x^T$ with $x^S \in S$ and $x^T \in T$; we call $x^S$
    84		(resp.\ $x^T$) the \emph{projection of $x$ onto $S$ parallel to $T$} (resp.\
    85		onto $T$ parallel to $S$). The unique linear map $L : V \to V$ with
    86		$x \mapsto x^S$ is the \emph{projector onto $S$ parallel to $T$}.
    87	\end{definition}
    88	
    89	A subspace may have many complementary subspaces: in $\F_2^2$, the subspace
    90	$S = \mathrm{span}\{(1,1)\}$ has the distinct complements
    91	$\mathrm{span}\{(1,0)\}$ and $\mathrm{span}\{(0,1)\}$. Given a basis of $S$,
    92	one may nevertheless single out a \emph{canonical} complement.
    93	
    94	% Unmarked, tracked in issue #667; no permanent exemption. `canonicalComplement` fixes the
    95	% pivot set by the intrinsic prefix-rank characterization instead of running the
    96	% reduced-row-echelon algorithm this node prescribes. The two agree by the
    97	% basis-independence paragraph below, but that identification is not itself formalized,
    98	% so a statement-level mark here would claim the algorithmic presentation as matched.
    99	\begin{definition}[Canonical complement]\label{def:canonical-complement}
   100		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.canonicalComplement}
   101		\uses{def:register-subspace}
   102		Let $\hat{E}$ be the standard basis of $V = \F^n$ and let
   103		$F = \{v_1, \dots, v_m\} \subset V$ be a set of $m$ linearly independent
   104		vectors. Write $v_i = \sum_{j=1}^n a_{i,j}\, \hat{e}_j$, and, using a
   105		canonical Gaussian-elimination algorithm valid over arbitrary fields,
   106		transform the $m \times n$ matrix $(a_{i,j})$ to reduced row echelon form
   107		$(b_{i,j})$. Let $J$ be the set of $m$ column indices containing the leading
   108		$1$ entry of each row of $(b_{i,j})$. The \emph{canonical complement of $F$}
   109		is the set of $n - m$ standard basis vectors
   110		\[
   111			F^\perp = \{\hat{e}_j : j \notin J\}\;.
   112		\]
   113		The canonical complement is a \emph{set} of vectors, not a subspace.
   114		% Basis-independence made explicit here: the source defines F^perp through
   115		% a basis but does not assert dependence on it; uniqueness of the reduced
   116		% row echelon form gives dependence on span(F) alone.
   117		Although defined through the basis $F$, it depends only on
   118		$\mathrm{span}(F)$ and the ambient standard basis: two bases of the same
   119		subspace form the rows of row-equivalent matrices, which have the same
   120		reduced row echelon form and hence the same pivot set $J$. The presentation
   121		through Gaussian elimination, adopted by \cite{Ji2020MIPStar}, makes the
   122		canonical complement efficiently computable. If $S$ is a register subspace
   123		spanned by $\hat{E}_0 \subseteq \hat{E}$, then the canonical complement of
   124		$\hat{E}_0$ is $\hat{E} \setminus \hat{E}_0$, and its span coincides with
   125		$S^\perp$.
   126	\end{definition}
   127	
   128	% Unmarked, tracked in issue #667, for the reason recorded above
   129	% Definition~def:canonical-complement. `isCompl_registerSubmodule_canonicalComplement`
   130	% proves exactly the displayed conclusion for the prefix-rank complement, and its own
   131	% docstring places the equivalence with a reduced-row-echelon algorithm outside the
   132	% statement; the proof below is the row-echelon route and is not the route Lean takes.
   133	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:canonical-complement}
   134		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.isCompl_registerSubmodule_canonicalComplement}
   135		\uses{def:canonical-complement, def:complementary}
   136		Let $S$ be the span of linearly independent vectors
   137		$F = \{v_1, \dots, v_m\} \subseteq V$, let $F^\perp$ be the canonical
   138		complement of $F$, and let $T = \mathrm{span}(F^\perp)$. Then
   139		\[
   140			S + T = V\;, \qquad S \cap T = \{0\}\;.
   141		\]
   142	\end{lemma}

   144		\uses{def:canonical-complement}

   198	\section{Finite fields, traces, and self-dual bases}
   199	% Paper labels sec:finite-fields, sec:subfields, sec:ff-representations kept
   200	% for cross-reference fidelity.
   201	\label{sec:finite-fields}
   202	\label{sec:subfields}
   203	\label{sec:ff-representations}
   204	
   205	Let $p$ be a prime and $q = p^k$ a prime power. We write $\F_p$ and $\F_q$ for
   206	the finite fields with $p$ and $q$ elements; $p$ is the characteristic of
   207	$\F_q$, and $\F_p$ is its prime subfield.
   208	
   209	\begin{definition}[Coordinate map and multiplication tables]\label{def:subfields-kappa}
   210		\lean{MIPStarRE.QPBT.chiOfBasis, MIPStarRE.QPBT.basisCoordVec}
   211		\leanok
   212		% The source lets k range over all integers; the extension field exists
   213		% only for k >= 1, so that domain condition is made explicit here.
   214		Let $q$ be a prime power and $k \ge 1$ an integer, so that $\F_q$ is a
   215		subfield of $\F_{q^k}$ and $\F_{q^k}$ is a linear space of dimension $k$
   216		over $\F_q$.
   217		Fix a basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$. The bijection
   218		$\kappa_q : \F_{q^k} \to \F_q^k$ associated with this basis is
   219		\[
   220			\kappa_q : a \mapsto (a_i)_{i=1}^k\;, \qquad

221			\text{where } a = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i e_i\;.
   222		\]
   223		The map $\kappa_q$ is an isomorphism of $\F_q$-vector spaces; in particular
   224		$\kappa_q(a + b) = \kappa_q(a) + \kappa_q(b)$ for all $a, b \in \F_{q^k}$.
   225		Moreover, multiplication by a fixed element corresponds to a linear map:
   226		for every $a \in \F_{q^k}$ there is a matrix $K_a \in \Mat_k(\F_q)$, the
   227		\emph{multiplication table of $a$ with respect to $\{e_i\}$}, such that
   228		$\kappa_q(ab) = K_a\, \kappa_q(b)$ for all $b \in \F_{q^k}$.
   229		The map extends coordinatewise to vectors, matrices, and sets: for
   230		$v = (v_1, \dots, v_n) \in \F_{q^k}^n$ set
   231		$\kappa_q(v) = (\kappa_q(v_i))_{i=1}^n \in \F_q^{kn}$; for

   371	\begin{definition}[Individual and total degree]\label{def:polynomials-degree}
   372		\uses{def:polyfunc}
   373		An $m$-variate polynomial $f$ over $\F_q$ is a function of the form
   374		\[
   375			f(x_1, \dots, x_m) = \sum_{\alpha \in \{0, 1, \dots, q-1\}^m}
   376			c_\alpha\, x_1^{\alpha_1} \cdots x_m^{\alpha_m}
   377		\]
   378		with coefficients $c_\alpha \in \F_q$; the coefficients are uniquely
   379		determined by $f$, since the $q^m$ monomial functions indexed by
   380		$\alpha \in \{0, 1, \dots, q-1\}^m$ span the $q^m$-dimensional space of all
   381		functions $\F_q^m \to \F_q$ and are therefore linearly independent. The
   382		polynomial $f$ has \emph{individual degree (at most) $d$} if
   383		$c_\alpha \neq 0$ only when $\alpha_i \le d$ for all $1 \le i \le m$, and
   384		\emph{total degree (at most) $d$} if $c_\alpha \neq 0$ only when
   385		$\sum_i \alpha_i \le d$. (Affine) \emph{multilinear} polynomials are those
   386		of individual degree $1$.
   387		% Relationship to def:polyfunc: polyfunc keeps polynomial representatives,
   388		% so evaluation identifies it with the function classes above only for
   389		% d <= q-1.
   390		Definition~\ref{def:polyfunc} introduces the set $\polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$ of
   391		polynomials in $\F_q[x_1, \dots, x_m]$ of degree at most $d$ in each
   392		variable, identified by their polynomial representatives rather than by the
   393		functions they induce. Evaluation maps $\polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$ onto the set of
   394		$m$-variate polynomials of individual degree at most $\min(d, q-1)$ in the
   395		sense above; for $d \le q-1$ this map is a bijection, while for $d \ge q$
   396		distinct representatives, such as $x_1^q$ and $x_1$, induce the same
   397		function. Statements phrased in terms of $\polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$ retain the
   398		representative convention of Definition~\ref{def:polyfunc}.
   399	\end{definition}

   401	\begin{lemma}[Schwartz--Zippel lemma~\cite{Sch80,Zip79}]\label{lem:schwartz-zippel}
   402		\lean{MIPStarRE.LDT.Preliminaries.schwartzZippel_totalDegree}
   403		\leanok
   404		% Restatement of lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree under the source's label.
   405		\uses{def:polynomials-degree}
   406		Let $f, g : \F_q^m \to \F_q$ be two unequal polynomials of total degree at
   407		most $d$. Then
   408		\[
   409			\Prb_{\bx \sim \F_q^m}[f(\bx) = g(\bx)] \le \frac{d}{q}\;.
   410		\]
   411	\end{lemma}
   412	\begin{proof}
   413		\leanok
   414		\uses{lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree}
   415		This is Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree}, stated and proved in
   416		Chapter~\ref{chap:preliminaries}; it is restated here under the label used
   417		by \cite{Ji2020MIPStar}.
   418	\end{proof}

   420	\begin{remark}\label{rem:schwartz-zippel-restated}
   421		Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel} restates the total-degree bound of
   422		Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree} under the label used by
   423		\cite{Ji2020MIPStar}. The individual-degree consequence,
   424		Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel-individual}, shows that distinct elements of
   425		$\polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$ agree on at most an $md/q$ fraction of the points of

   427		individual-degree form.
   428	\end{remark}

   431	error-correcting code with good distance, the \emph{low-degree code} (a special
   432	case of the generalized Reed--Muller code).

   498	\begin{definition}[Lines]\label{def:line}

   500		$(u,v) \in (\F_q^m)^2$ is the subset

   505		is explicitly allowed, in which case the line is the singleton $\{u\}$. A
   506		line $\ell(u,v)$ is \emph{axis-parallel} if there is a coordinate
   507		$i \in \{1, \dots, m\}$ for which $v = e_i$, the $i$-th elementary basis
   508		vector of $\F_q^m$; such a line is said to be \emph{parallel to the $i$-th
   509		direction}. A line $\ell(u,v)$ is \emph{diagonal} if there exists
   510		$i \in \{0, 1, \dots, m-1\}$ such that $v_1 = v_2 = \dots = v_i = 0$ (for
   511		$i = 0$ the condition is vacuous, so every line is diagonal).

def IsDualBasisPair {F K ι : Type*} [CommRing F] [CommRing K] [DecidableEq ι]
    [Algebra F K] (b b' : Module.Basis ι F K) : Prop :=
  ∀ i j, Algebra.trace F K (b i * b' j) = if i = j then 1 else 0

namespace Basis

/-- Self-duality in blueprint
`def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis`, paper `04_preliminaries.tex:494-497`. -/
def IsSelfDual {F K ι : Type*} [CommRing F] [CommRing K] [DecidableEq ι]
    [Algebra F K] (b : Module.Basis ι F K) : Prop :=
  IsDualBasisPair b b

/-- Normality in blueprint
`def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis`, paper `04_preliminaries.tex:498-502`. The
Frobenius exponent uses the cardinality of the base field. -/
def IsNormal {F K : Type*} [CommSemiring F] [Fintype F] [Field K] [Algebra F K]
    {k : ℕ} (b : Module.Basis (Fin k) F K) : Prop :=
  ∃ α : K, ∀ j, b j = α ^ (Fintype.card F ^ j.1)

end Basis

  /--

  representation_natural :
    ∀ v : Fin basisDim → ZMod 2,
      (toFieldModel.equiv (basis.equivFun.symm v)).val =

  /-- Self-duality of the chosen basis with respect to the field trace. -/
  selfDual : ∀ i j, Algebra.trace (ZMod 2) K (basis i * basis j) =
    if i = j then 1 else 0
  /-- Normality of the chosen basis, recorded by a Frobenius generator. -/
  normal : ∃ α : K, ∀ i, basis i = α ^ (2 ^ i.1)
